units.title: Sampling and Quantisation
units.tip: To store a real-world signal in a computer, you must sample it at discrete times and round the values to discrete levels. Sampling captures snapshots, quantisation limits the precision, and both introduce information loss.

exercises.question: What is sampling in signal processing?
exercises.answer: Taking measurements of a continuous signal at specific time intervals
exercises.explain: Sampling converts a continuous signal into a discrete sequence by measuring it at regular times. The distance between samples is determined by the sampling rate.
choices: Taking measurements of a continuous signal at specific time intervals
Reducing noise from a signal
Storing an entire signal in memory at once
Converting analog audio to speakers

exercises.question: What is the sampling rate or sampling frequency?
exercises.answer: The number of samples taken per second, measured in Hertz
exercises.explain: Sampling rate is how many times per second you measure the signal. Audio CDs use 44.1 kHz (44,100 samples per second). Higher rates capture faster changes.
choices: The time between samples in milliseconds
The number of samples taken per second, measured in Hertz
The error introduced by sampling
The volume level of a sample

exercises.question: If a signal is sampled at 48 kHz, how many samples are taken per second?
exercises.explain: A sampling rate of 48 kHz means 48,000 samples are taken every second. The kilohertz unit means thousands of cycles per second.

exercises.question: What is the sampling period?
exercises.answer: The time between consecutive samples
exercises.explain: Sampling period is 1 divided by the sampling rate. For 44.1 kHz, the period is about 22.7 microseconds. Higher rates mean shorter periods.
choices: The time between consecutive samples
The total duration of the signal
The rate at which samples are taken
The number of bits per sample

exercises.question: What happens to information about rapid changes when you sample slowly?
exercises.answer: The rapid changes are not captured in the samples
exercises.explain: If a signal changes quickly but you sample slowly, you miss the rapid variations. You only record values at your sample times, losing what happens between samples.
choices: The rapid changes are amplified
The rapid changes are not captured in the samples
The rapid changes are smoothed out by filtering
The sampling rate automatically increases

exercises.question: What is quantisation?
exercises.answer: Rounding continuous signal values to discrete levels for storage
exercises.explain: Quantisation converts the infinite precision of an analog signal into a finite set of discrete values. This introduces quantisation error but allows digital storage.
choices: Measuring the strength of a signal
Removing high-frequency noise from a signal
Rounding continuous signal values to discrete levels for storage
Determining when to sample a signal

exercises.question: What is bit depth?
exercises.answer: The number of bits used to represent each sample value
exercises.explain: Bit depth determines how many discrete levels are available. 16-bit audio has 65,536 possible values per sample (2^16). Higher bit depth means finer resolution.
choices: The number of bits used to represent each sample value
The sampling rate in bits per second
The speed of digital signal processing
The total storage in megabytes

exercises.question: How many distinct levels can an 8-bit sample represent?
exercises.explain: With 8 bits, you can represent 2^8 = 256 different values. This is common for audio and image pixels, but provides less precision than 16-bit.

exercises.question: What is quantisation error?
exercises.answer: The difference between the true signal value and the rounded quantised value
exercises.explain: Quantisation error is the noise introduced by rounding. You can only represent discrete levels, so continuous values must be rounded to the nearest level.
choices: The difference between the true signal value and the rounded quantised value
Errors from filtering the signal
Errors from sampling too slowly
Errors in the recording device

exercises.question: How does increasing bit depth affect quantisation error?
exercises.answer: Quantisation error decreases because more discrete levels are available
exercises.explain: With more bits, you have more discrete levels to choose from, so you can round to a closer level. This reduces the maximum error per sample.
choices: Quantisation error stays the same
Quantisation error becomes unpredictable
Quantisation error decreases because more discrete levels are available
Quantisation error increases

units.title: The Sampling Theorem and Aliasing
units.tip: The Nyquist sampling theorem tells you the minimum sample rate needed to capture a signal without information loss. Sample too slowly and high frequencies fold down to create aliasing.

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist sampling theorem?
exercises.answer: A signal must be sampled at twice the highest frequency it contains
exercises.explain: To accurately capture a signal without loss, your sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency present. This is called the Nyquist rate.
choices: A signal must be sampled at twice the highest frequency it contains
A signal must be quantised to 16 bits minimum
A signal loses quality when sampled at all
A signal can be sampled at any rate and still be accurate

exercises.question: What is the Nyquist frequency?
exercises.answer: Half the sampling rate, the highest frequency that can be accurately captured
exercises.explain: The Nyquist frequency is the maximum frequency your sampled signal can represent. For a 44.1 kHz sample rate, the Nyquist frequency is 22.05 kHz.
choices: The rate at which samples are taken
The frequency of quantisation error
Half the sampling rate, the highest frequency that can be accurately captured
The lowest frequency in a signal

exercises.question: For a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz, what is the Nyquist frequency?
exercises.explain: The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate: 44.1 kHz / 2 = 22.05 kHz. This is why audio CDs at 44.1 kHz can capture frequencies up to about 22 kHz.
choices: 88.2 kHz
44.1 kHz

exercises.question: If a signal contains a 10 kHz component, what is the minimum sampling rate needed?
exercises.answer: 20 kHz
exercises.explain: By the Nyquist theorem, you must sample at twice the highest frequency. For 10 kHz, you need at least 20 kHz (20,000 samples per second).
choices: 10 kHz
20 kHz
5 kHz
40 kHz

exercises.question: What happens if you sample below the Nyquist rate?
exercises.answer: Information is lost and cannot be recovered from the samples
exercises.explain: Sampling below the Nyquist rate is called undersampling. The original signal cannot be perfectly reconstructed from the samples because information about high frequencies is lost.
choices: The sampling rate automatically increases
Information is lost and cannot be recovered from the samples
Quantisation error increases instead
The signal is automatically filtered

exercises.question: What is aliasing in signal processing?
exercises.answer: High frequencies being misrepresented as lower frequencies due to undersampling
exercises.explain: Aliasing happens when a signal is sampled too slowly. High-frequency components get folded down and appear as false lower-frequency signals in the samples.
choices: Quantising a signal to lower bit depth
Filtering a signal to remove noise
High frequencies being misrepresented as lower frequencies due to undersampling
Using a different name for a signal

exercises.question: When a 50 kHz signal is sampled at 40 kHz, what frequency does it alias to?
exercises.answer: 10 kHz
exercises.explain: Sampling at 40 kHz repeats the spectrum every 40 kHz, so 50 kHz looks the same as 50 - 40 = 10 kHz. Equivalently, it is 30 kHz above the 20 kHz Nyquist frequency, so it folds back to 20 - 30 = -10 kHz, which appears as 10 kHz.
choices: 50 kHz
10 kHz
40 kHz
5 kHz

exercises.question: What is an anti-aliasing filter?
exercises.answer: A low-pass filter applied before sampling to remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency
exercises.explain: An anti-aliasing filter removes high frequencies before sampling. This prevents those frequencies from folding down and creating false signals in the sampled data.
choices: A filter applied after sampling to recover lost frequencies
A filter that removes all frequencies below 20 kHz
A device that increases the sampling rate automatically
A low-pass filter applied before sampling to remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency

exercises.question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter necessary before sampling audio?
exercises.answer: To remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency that would otherwise create audible artifacts
exercises.explain: Without an anti-aliasing filter, high frequencies in the input fold down to audible lower frequencies, creating a distorted or 'metallic' sound. The filter removes these high frequencies before sampling.
choices: To improve sound quality by removing all noise
To reduce the storage space needed for audio
To make the sampling rate unnecessary
To remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency that would otherwise create audible artifacts

exercises.question: If you sample at 48 kHz without an anti-aliasing filter, what is the highest frequency that will not alias?
exercises.answer: 24 kHz
exercises.explain: The Nyquist frequency at 48 kHz is 24 kHz. Any frequency above 24 kHz will alias. Without filtering, those high frequencies create false signals in the 0-24 kHz range.
choices: 96 kHz
24 kHz
48 kHz
12 kHz

units.title: Discrete-Time Signals
units.tip: A discrete-time signal is a sequence of numbers, one for each sample. You can analyse it with operations like convolution and apply transforms to understand its frequency content.

exercises.question: What is a discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: A sequence of numbers indexed by sample number or time
exercises.explain: A discrete-time signal is written as x[n] where n is the sample index. After sampling, the continuous-time signal becomes a sequence of values.
choices: A frequency-domain representation
A sequence of numbers indexed by sample number or time
A continuous waveform without sampling
The output of a quantiser only

exercises.question: What does the notation x[n] represent?
exercises.answer: The value of signal x at sample number n
exercises.explain: In discrete-time notation, x[n] is the signal value at the n-th sample. This is used instead of x(t) for continuous signals, where t is time.
choices: The maximum value of the signal
The frequency of the signal
The value of signal x at sample number n
The number of samples in the signal

exercises.question: What is signal scaling?
exercises.answer: Multiplying each sample by a constant to change amplitude
exercises.explain: Scaling by a constant c means computing y[n] = c * x[n]. Scaling by 0.5 halves the amplitude; scaling by 2 doubles it.
choices: Filtering out low frequencies
Changing the sampling rate
Multiplying each sample by a constant to change amplitude
Shifting the signal in time

exercises.question: What does it mean to add two discrete-time signals?
exercises.answer: Adding corresponding samples: y[n] = x1[n] + x2[n]
exercises.explain: Signal addition is sample-by-sample: the n-th output sample is the sum of the n-th samples from both input signals. This is useful for mixing signals.
choices: Concatenating the samples end-to-end
Multiplying all samples together
Adding corresponding samples: y[n] = x1[n] + x2[n]
Replacing one signal with the other

exercises.question: What does it mean to shift a discrete-time signal in time?
exercises.answer: Moving the signal forward or backward by delaying or advancing samples
exercises.explain: A time shift by M samples gives y[n] = x[n - M]. If M is positive, the signal is delayed; if negative, advanced.
choices: Changing the frequency content of the signal
Scaling the signal amplitude
Adding white noise to the signal
Moving the signal forward or backward by delaying or advancing samples

exercises.question: What is the length of a discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: The number of samples in the sequence
exercises.explain: Signal length is how many data points the signal contains. A 1-second audio clip at 44.1 kHz has a length of 44,100 samples.
choices: The duration of the signal in seconds
The highest frequency in the signal
The sampling rate used
The number of samples in the sequence

exercises.question: What is the energy of a discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: The sum of the squares of all sample values
exercises.explain: Signal energy is the sum of x[n]^2 over all n. It is useful for measuring how strong a signal is and for normalisation.
choices: The average of all sample values
The product of all sample values
The highest sample value
The sum of the squares of all sample values

exercises.question: What is a periodic discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: A signal that repeats with a fixed period N, where x[n] = x[n + N]
exercises.explain: A periodic signal repeats exactly every N samples. The smallest N for which this is true is the period. Many signals in DSP are periodic.
choices: A signal that repeats with a fixed period N, where x[n] = x[n + N]
A signal with only one frequency component
A signal with zero mean
A signal that never repeats

exercises.question: What is the mean (average) of a discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: The sum of all samples divided by the number of samples
exercises.explain: The mean is calculated as (1/N) * sum of x[n]. It represents the DC (constant) component of the signal.
choices: The value that appears most often
The highest sample value
The middle value when samples are sorted
The sum of all samples divided by the number of samples

exercises.question: What is a causal discrete-time signal?
exercises.answer: A signal that is zero for all negative time indices, x[n] = 0 for n < 0
exercises.explain: A causal signal only has values at n >= 0. This models real-world signals that start at a specific time and do not have a past before that.
choices: A signal that is zero for all negative time indices, x[n] = 0 for n < 0
A signal with a specific frequency content
A signal with maximum energy
A signal with periodic repetition

units.title: The DFT and FFT
units.tip: The Discrete Fourier Transform converts a signal from the time domain to the frequency domain, showing what frequencies are present. The Fast Fourier Transform is an efficient algorithm for computing it.

exercises.question: What is the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)?
exercises.answer: A transform that converts a discrete-time signal from time domain to frequency domain
exercises.explain: The DFT shows what frequencies are present in a signal and their strengths. It converts a sequence of time samples into a sequence of frequency components.
choices: A way to compress audio files
A sampling technique
A transform that converts a discrete-time signal from time domain to frequency domain
A method for removing noise

exercises.question: What does the time domain show?
exercises.answer: The signal value at each point in time
exercises.explain: The time domain is the original representation: samples x[n] plotted against time or sample index. It shows what the signal looks like as it evolves.
choices: The frequencies present in a signal
The energy at each frequency
The signal value at each point in time
The rate of change of the signal

exercises.question: What does the frequency domain show?
exercises.answer: The strength of each frequency component in a signal
exercises.explain: The frequency domain, output by the DFT, shows the magnitude and phase of each frequency. It tells you which frequencies are present and how strong they are.
choices: The sampling rate used
The time at which each sample occurs
The strength of each frequency component in a signal
The signal values in order

exercises.question: If a discrete signal has N samples, how many frequency components does its DFT have?
exercises.answer: N
exercises.explain: The DFT of an N-sample signal produces N frequency components. Each component corresponds to a different frequency bin.
choices: 2N
N

exercises.question: What is the inverse DFT?
exercises.answer: A transform that converts frequency-domain data back to the time domain
exercises.explain: The inverse DFT (IDFT) reconstructs the original time-domain signal from its frequency components. Together, DFT and IDFT allow conversion between domains.
choices: An operation that removes frequencies
An alternative to the DFT for complex signals
A transform that converts frequency-domain data back to the time domain
A method to increase frequency resolution

exercises.question: What is the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)?
exercises.answer: An efficient algorithm for computing the DFT quickly
exercises.explain: The FFT is a clever algorithm that reduces the computation needed to calculate the DFT. Without it, processing large signals would be impractically slow.
choices: A method to remove high frequencies
An alternative to sampling
An efficient algorithm for computing the DFT quickly
A more accurate version of the DFT

exercises.question: How many multiplications does a naive DFT require for N samples?
exercises.answer: About N squared (N^2)
exercises.explain: A direct DFT computation requires roughly N^2 operations. For N = 1024, that is over 1 million operations. This is impractical for real-time audio.
choices: About N squared (N^2)
N
2N
Log(N)

exercises.question: How many multiplications does the FFT require for N samples?
exercises.answer: About N log(N)
exercises.explain: The FFT reduces complexity to roughly N log(N) operations. For N = 1024, that is about 10,000 operations, roughly 100 times faster than the naive DFT.
choices: N
About N log(N)
2N
N squared

exercises.question: Why does the FFT work efficiently?
exercises.answer: It exploits symmetries in the DFT computation to avoid redundant calculations
exercises.explain: The FFT uses divide-and-conquer and exploits the periodic nature of complex exponentials. It breaks the problem into smaller subproblems that share intermediate results.
choices: It uses a different mathematical formula
It is a statistical approximation of the DFT
It exploits symmetries in the DFT computation to avoid redundant calculations
It uses lower precision arithmetic

exercises.question: What is the Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm?
exercises.answer: A divide-and-conquer algorithm that recursively decomposes the DFT into smaller DFTs
exercises.explain: The Cooley-Tukey algorithm, published in 1965, is the most common FFT method. It works best when the signal length N is a power of 2.
choices: A divide-and-conquer algorithm that recursively decomposes the DFT into smaller DFTs
A quantisation technique for the frequency domain
A method for removing aliasing
An alternative to the DFT for real-time processing

units.title: Filters and Convolution
units.tip: Filters modify signals by enhancing or removing frequency components. Convolution is the mathematical operation that applies a filter. FIR filters are finite impulse response, IIR filters have feedback. Windowing reduces spectral leakage.

lessons.title: FIR vs IIR Filters and Convolution

exercises.question: What is a digital filter?
exercises.answer: A mathematical operation that selectively amplifies or attenuates frequencies in a signal
exercises.explain: A digital filter processes a signal to enhance some frequencies and reduce others. Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, and band-stop are common types.
choices: A physical device for sound quality
A method for sampling signals
Analog circuits used in computers
A mathematical operation that selectively amplifies or attenuates frequencies in a signal

exercises.question: What is an FIR filter?
exercises.answer: A Finite Impulse Response filter that depends only on current and past input samples
exercises.explain: An FIR filter has a finite number of non-zero coefficients and depends only on past inputs: y[n] = b0*x[n] + b1*x[n-1] + b2*x[n-2] + ... It is always stable.
choices: A filter that uses infinite past input samples
A filter used only for high frequencies
A Finite Impulse Response filter that depends only on current and past input samples
An analog circuit used in recording

exercises.question: What is an IIR filter?
exercises.answer: An Infinite Impulse Response filter that uses both input and feedback from past outputs
exercises.explain: An IIR filter has feedback: y[n] = b0*x[n] + b1*x[n-1] + ... - a1*y[n-1] - a2*y[n-2] - ... It can be more efficient than FIR but can become unstable if not designed carefully.
choices: A type of sampling method
A filter with no feedback
An Infinite Impulse Response filter that uses both input and feedback from past outputs
A filter that removes all frequencies above 1 kHz

exercises.question: What is convolution in signal processing?
exercises.answer: A mathematical operation that applies a filter to a signal by sliding and multiplying
exercises.explain: Convolution combines a signal with a filter kernel. Each output sample is the sum of products of the signal and filter coefficients, like a weighted average sliding along the signal.
choices: A method for removing noise using the Fourier transform
A sampling technique for reducing aliasing
An alternative to the DFT
A mathematical operation that applies a filter to a signal by sliding and multiplying

exercises.question: When implementing a digital filter in code, what does an FIR filter require?
exercises.answer: Storage for a buffer of past input samples and coefficients
exercises.explain: An FIR filter maintains a delay line (buffer) of past input samples. As new samples arrive, you compute the weighted sum and shift the buffer.
choices: Storage for a buffer of past input samples and coefficients
The entire signal in memory at once
A real-time FFT computation at every sample
Recursive calculations that depend on previous output

exercises.question: What is a low-pass filter?
exercises.answer: A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies
exercises.explain: A low-pass filter allows frequencies below a cutoff to pass through and reduces frequencies above the cutoff. It smooths signals and removes high-frequency noise.
choices: A filter applied only during sampling
A filter that removes all frequencies
A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies
A filter that amplifies frequencies near the Nyquist rate

exercises.question: What is a high-pass filter?
exercises.answer: A filter that passes high frequencies and attenuates low frequencies
exercises.explain: A high-pass filter removes low-frequency components, such as DC offset and slow drift. It allows rapid changes to pass through.
choices: A filter that passes high frequencies and attenuates low frequencies
A filter that removes all frequencies
A filter that equalises all frequencies
A filter that only passes frequencies above the Nyquist rate

exercises.question: What is windowing in the context of filter design?
exercises.answer: Multiplying a filter kernel by a window function to reduce spectral leakage
exercises.explain: A window function tapers the filter coefficients toward zero at the edges, reducing ripple and spectral leakage. Hamming, Hann, and Blackman are common windows.
choices: Multiplying a filter kernel by a window function to reduce spectral leakage
Removing silent portions of a signal
Limiting the filter to process only a portion of the signal
Adjusting the cutoff frequency of a filter

exercises.question: What is spectral leakage?
exercises.answer: Energy from one frequency spilling into adjacent frequency bins during analysis
exercises.explain: Spectral leakage occurs when a signal does not fit exactly into the FFT bins. The rectangular window inherently causes leakage. Windowing reduces it.
choices: Losing frequency information when the sampling rate is too low
Aliasing of high frequencies
Energy from one frequency spilling into adjacent frequency bins during analysis
The main lobe of a frequency response

exercises.question: What is the cutoff frequency of a filter?
exercises.answer: The frequency at which the filter transitions from pass band to stop band
exercises.explain: The cutoff frequency (or corner frequency) is where the filter gain drops to 70.7% (-3 dB). It marks the boundary between frequencies that pass and those that are attenuated.
choices: The frequency with the most energy
The frequency at which the filter transitions from pass band to stop band
The Nyquist frequency of the signal
The highest frequency in the input signal

units.title: Applications in Audio and Images
units.tip: Digital signal processing is essential in audio recording, compression, effects, and image processing. The same principles apply across domains: filtering, Fourier analysis, and convolution.

exercises.question: What does lossy audio compression such as MP3 do?
exercises.answer: Shrinks the file by discarding detail that is hard for listeners to hear
exercises.explain: Lossy compression uses psychoacoustics: detail humans hear poorly is discarded to save space. Lossless formats such as FLAC keep every sample and shrink the file without discarding anything.
choices: Limiting the frequency range to 20 Hz to 20 kHz
Applying a high-pass filter
Reducing the volume of audio
Shrinks the file by discarding detail that is hard for listeners to hear

exercises.question: What is a graphic equaliser?
exercises.answer: A tool that uses multiple filters to boost or cut specific frequency bands
exercises.explain: A graphic EQ divides the audio spectrum into bands (bass, mids, treble) and allows adjustment of each. It uses multiple filters working in parallel.
choices: A tool that uses multiple filters to boost or cut specific frequency bands
A tool for recording audio
A device that measures sound intensity
A type of speaker

exercises.question: How does an audio reverb effect use convolution?
exercises.answer: Convolving the input signal with an impulse response recorded from an acoustic space
exercises.explain: Convolution reverb convolves the dry signal with the impulse response of a real room. This simulates the reflections and resonances of that space.
choices: By multiplying the signal by a constant factor
Convolving the input signal with an impulse response recorded from an acoustic space
By applying a high-pass filter repeatedly
By delaying the signal by a fixed amount

exercises.question: What is an impulse response in audio?
exercises.answer: The output of a system when given a brief, sharp input signal
exercises.explain: An impulse response characterises how a system (room, speaker, microphone) affects sound. It captures the system's behaviour completely and is used in convolution reverb.
choices: The delay between input and output
The output of a system when given a brief, sharp input signal
The volume increase when audio is compressed
The frequency response of a speaker

exercises.question: How do noise-cancelling headphones use DSP?
exercises.answer: By playing an inverted copy of the ambient noise so the two cancel out
exercises.explain: Microphones pick up ambient sound, a filter (often adaptive) produces an inverted copy, and the speaker plays it. The two waves are in opposite phase, so destructive interference reduces the noise.
choices: By using a very high sampling rate
By playing an inverted copy of the ambient noise so the two cancel out
By increasing the volume of the desired signal
By removing all frequencies above a cutoff

exercises.question: How does image filtering relate to audio filtering?
exercises.answer: Both use convolution; audio is 1D, images are 2D
exercises.explain: Image filters apply convolution with a 2D kernel (small matrix) to produce effects like blur, sharpening, or edge detection. The mathematics is the same as audio filtering.
choices: Audio filtering uses FFT, image filtering does not
They are completely unrelated
Image filtering is slower than audio filtering
Both use convolution; audio is 1D, images are 2D

exercises.question: What does a blur filter do?
exercises.answer: Applies a weighted average over a neighbourhood of pixels to smooth the image
exercises.explain: A blur filter uses a kernel with positive coefficients that average nearby pixels. This reduces sharp transitions and noise but also removes detail.
choices: Applies a weighted average over a neighbourhood of pixels to smooth the image
Increases the contrast of the image
Removes all low frequencies
Detects edges in the image

exercises.question: What does an edge-detection filter do?
exercises.answer: Highlights areas where pixel values change rapidly
exercises.explain: Edge detection filters, like Sobel or Laplacian, amplify regions where the image changes sharply (edges). They suppress uniform areas.
choices: Highlights areas where pixel values change rapidly
Removes all edges from the image
Inverts the colours of the image
Smooths the image uniformly

exercises.question: How is the 2D Fourier Transform used in image processing?
exercises.answer: To analyse the frequency content of an image in the horizontal and vertical directions
exercises.explain: The 2D FFT decomposes an image into its spatial frequencies. Low frequencies represent overall brightness; high frequencies represent edges and detail.
choices: To analyse the frequency content of an image in the horizontal and vertical directions
To remove all colour information
To compress images without loss
To convert the image to grayscale

exercises.question: What is downsampling in image processing?
exercises.answer: Reducing the resolution by keeping fewer pixels, usually using a low-pass filter first
exercises.explain: Downsampling reduces image size. To avoid aliasing, a low-pass filter is applied first to remove detail above the new Nyquist frequency.
choices: Reducing the resolution by keeping fewer pixels, usually using a low-pass filter first
Converting to a different colour space
Increasing the brightness of the image
Applying a sharpen filter
